title: AWS DevOps Agent
subtitle: Operational evidence → controlled action
scenario: Checkout 5xx investigation and retry-policy release review

slides.title: AWS DevOps Agent
slides.takeaway: Investigations produce hypotheses and evidence for operational review.
slides.notes: Open with the operational job, not a claim of full autonomy. A checkout service is failing after a deployment. We want a coherent investigation, a defensible mitigation decision, and a follow-up item that prevents recurrence. Production operations are generally available; release-management features are preview. The examples in this deck are proposed exercises. The demo slots include the operator walkthrough and a prepared-result fallback, not a promise that an agent run completes within the allotted minutes.
slides.label: Operations / SRE / Platform engineering

slides.title: Define the incident scope and evidence window
slides.takeaway: A time window, a service boundary, and a change reference make the question answerable.
slides.notes: Use the checkout incident as the thread through this presentation. Supply an incident window and the deployment identity before asking for a cause. A production symptom, an agent hypothesis, a mitigation plan, and a verified recovery are different artifacts. The example does not assert that a real incident occurred. The on-call engineer remains responsible for triage and for comparing conclusions with the source systems.

items.title: Signal
items.body: Checkout 5xx errors rise after a release.

items.title: Scope
items.body: Service, environment, UTC window, deployment SHA.

items.title: Investigation
items.body: Correlate telemetry and changes; expose missing evidence.

items.title: Decision
items.body: Accept or reject the hypothesis; choose a safe next action.

slides.title: Operational capability groups and their dependencies
slides.takeaway: Choose an operational job first; enable its data and action paths second.
slides.notes: The capability map separates incident work, on-demand operational questions, prevention, configured recurring tasks, and release validation. They share application context but differ in invocation and output. A daily summary is a custom-agent configuration, not an automatically provisioned SRE dashboard. Release management is a separate preview track and should not inherit the availability label of production operations.

items.title: Investigate incidents
items.body: Triage related signals and produce findings and mitigation guidance.

items.title: Ask operational questions
items.body: Inspect resources, alarms, health, and prior investigations.

items.title: Prevent recurrence
items.body: Review patterns and prioritize reliability improvements.

items.title: Run custom tasks
items.body: Define a prompt, select tools/skills, and add a schedule.

items.title: Review release risk
items.body: Readiness reviews plus optional managed verification.

items.title: Test a deployed release
items.body: Explore a staging web application or REST API.

slides.title: Configure Agent Space data access and scope
slides.takeaway: Acceptance: one known resource is visible; an out-of-scope test resource is denied.
slides.notes: An Agent Space groups the context and integrations used for operational work. It is not an authorization boundary merely because it has a service name. IAM roles and integration permissions establish actual access. For the initial pilot, connect one service and inspect whether its deployment events, logs, and metrics can be read. Do not grant broad writes to compensate for missing read evidence. Private integrations need an explicit network connection; they are not reachable simply because a repository or tool is named in chat.
actions: Discover relationships and collect permitted evidence
Connect private tools explicitly when required
outputs: Known evidence coverage and documented gaps

slides.title: Investigate a service incident and review hypotheses
slides.takeaway: Acceptance: distinguish observed facts, hypotheses, and missing telemetry.
slides.notes: The agent can start from a manual request or a configured external trigger. As evidence arrives, the operator can steer the investigation toward a hypothesis or data source. That is useful when a dashboard and a deployment suggest different explanations. Ask for the evidence behind a conclusion and for alternatives that remain unresolved. A confident root-cause statement is not sufficient to close an incident.
inputs: Manual incident description, ticket or webhook
Time window, alarm and suspected change
actions: Collect findings; accept operator steering and feedback
outputs: Candidate cause and proposed mitigation plan

slides.title: Demo 1 · investigate checkout 5xx errors
slides.takeaway: Use a controlled incident snapshot; keep the investigation read-focused.
slides.notes: This seven-minute slot demonstrates the investigation workflow and the engineer’s judgment. It does not measure incident-response speed. Start a fresh request only if the environment is ready. The completed-run fallback must contain genuine, sanitized evidence from an authorized rehearsal; a schematic illustration must be labeled as such. No production mutation is required for this demo.
slides.prompt: Investigate the checkout 5xx increase in the supplied UTC window after the deployment. Cite telemetry and the deployed diff. Separate observed facts, competing hypotheses, and missing data. Propose a mitigation; do not change resources.
steps: Confirm scope
Open the Agent Space, incident window and deployment reference.
Inspect the investigation
Start or open a pre-run investigation; check source coverage.
Challenge the leading hypothesis
Compare two source observations and inspect a competing explanation.
Review mitigation
Check blast radius, rollback assumptions and missing evidence.
Record the handoff
Capture owner, evidence links, next action and verification check.
slides.success: One source-backed hypothesis and one reviewable next action—not an asserted diagnosis.
slides.preflight: Prepare a sanitized incident snapshot, read access and a completed investigation before presenting.
slides.fallback: After 60 seconds without usable output, use the completed run and inspect its evidence; do not wait for a fresh run.

slides.title: Daily service-health and incident queries
slides.takeaway: Acceptance: inspect one cited alarm or resource before sharing the summary.
slides.notes: Not every operational task is an incident. The on-demand interface can answer focused questions about service health, resource configuration, recent alarms and investigation history. Ask for a specific period rather than “is everything healthy.” The value is an evidence-linked summary that reduces console navigation. Where a source is unavailable, the answer should state the gap rather than imply coverage.
inputs: A bounded question and time interval
actions: Query health, alarms and deployment history
Summarize investigations and create report artifacts
outputs: A reusable incident or service-report artifact

slides.title: Create prevention tasks from investigation history
slides.takeaway: Acceptance: an owner and a measurable recurrence or detection check accompany each accepted item.
slides.notes: Prevention analyzes investigation history and produces recommendations. It is not a guarantee that failures will disappear. Keep recommendations separate from accepted engineering work: a team must assess relevance, assign ownership and decide how to validate an improvement. Use a known repeat incident to show how the suggested change would make detection earlier or the service more resilient.
inputs: Team priorities and existing improvement backlog
actions: Evaluate recurring patterns on demand or on a schedule
Categorize observability, infrastructure, governance and code opportunities
outputs: Implementation context for an owned engineering task

slides.title: Configure scheduled operational reports
slides.takeaway: Acceptance: the selected tools—not the prompt alone—bound access and side effects.
slides.notes: A custom agent is a configured workflow. For example, a team can define a daily summary that reads alarms and recent investigations and returns an actionable report. Select only the tools needed for that job. A prompt that says “read only” does not neutralize a write-capable integration. Review the output and invocation record before enabling a recurring schedule.
inputs: A system prompt, selected tools and skills
An on-demand trigger or configured schedule
actions: Run a bounded multi-step operational task
Record tool use and outputs for each invocation
outputs: Daily health report or configuration-review artifact
Traceable run history for operator inspection

slides.title: Mitigation recommendations and action authorization
slides.takeaway: Directed actions have their own enablement, role, tool and approval path.
slides.notes: Keep the read-oriented investigation path separate from directed actions. Directed actions are disabled by default. Enabling them is only one layer: the relevant account role or third-party tool configuration must also permit the operation, and the operator must approve the concrete action. Review the target, parameters, blast radius and rollback plan. The release-testing write path is a different mechanism; do not assume this approval model protects application endpoints exercised by a test.

items.title: Propose
items.body: Agent identifies an operation, target and risk.

items.title: Enable + scope
items.body: Agent Space, elevated role and applicable tool controls.

items.title: Approve
items.body: Operator approves this operation at execution time.

items.title: Verify
items.body: Inspect audit evidence and the resulting service state.

slides.title: Release-review and deployed-application testing differ
slides.takeaway: Managed code verification is not the same as active testing against a deployed application.
slides.notes: Readiness review evaluates a change and can build and test it in a managed verification environment. Active release testing sends traffic to a running application and may perform POST, PUT and DELETE requests. Those operations can trigger real business effects. Use a disposable staging deployment, test identities and disabled external side effects. Both features remain a preview track in the documented Region. A positive review is evidence for the release owner, not a production deployment authorization.

left.title: Readiness review
left.body: Connected PR/MR or on-demand change → standards, dependencies and access-control review → findings plus optional build/test evidence.

right.title: Active release testing
right.body: Configured staging URL and test intent → browser or REST exploration → failures, reproduction steps and suggested fixes.

slides.callout: Safety distinction: testing can mutate application data even when infrastructure actions are not enabled.

slides.title: Demo 2 · review a risky release
slides.takeaway: A proposed retry-policy and database-timeout change must produce inspectable release evidence.
slides.notes: This five-minute walkthrough demonstrates interpretation rather than a fresh end-to-end run. The reviewed revision must match the displayed diff. Build failures caused by missing private dependencies are setup failures, not proof that the proposed application change is unsafe. Conversely, a skipped verification step is not a pass. Keep the production release decision with the existing owner.
slides.prompt: Review this change for dependency impact, retry amplification, database saturation and rollback viability. Cite affected code and verification evidence. Return risks and missing checks. Do not deploy or promote.
steps: Select the change
Show the PR/MR and its exact commit.
Start or open review
Confirm preview Region and enabled review/verification settings.
Inspect risk evidence
Trace a finding to changed code and a dependency.
Read verification
Separate a passed check, an unrun check and a failure.
Decide the next step
Release owner accepts, requests work or blocks promotion.
slides.success: Findings are tied to the exact change, and unexecuted checks are visible.
slides.preflight: Use a connected test repository and a pre-completed readiness review; do not point a test profile at production.
slides.fallback: Use the prepared review and code diff if the preview or verification environment is unavailable.

slides.title: Access operational context from coding clients
slides.takeaway: Acceptance: client connectivity does not widen the Agent Space’s permissions.
slides.notes: The documented remote MCP interface brings operational questions into a development environment. This can reduce the copy-and-paste handoff between an on-call engineer and a developer. It does not mean every AWS frontier agent shares one session or identity. Authenticate the client, scope access and preserve links to the original investigation. A2A and other access methods are integration building blocks, not a turnkey four-product orchestrator.
inputs: An authorized Agent Space and client identity
A concrete incident or operational question
actions: Connect an MCP-capable IDE or CLI to the remote server
Retrieve operational context through the configured interface
outputs: Investigation context next to repository work
A reviewable task or change proposal

slides.title: Kiro capabilities are separate from DevOps Agent
slides.takeaway: Kiro supports code work; the team still owns CI, IaC and operational correctness.
slides.notes: The original report included related developer tasks, so keep them visible without attributing them to the wrong product. Repository explanation, scoped code changes and test creation fit Kiro’s documented coding tools. IaC drafting, supplied-build-log diagnosis and runbook writing are composed uses of those tools. They are not native promises of complete infrastructure validation or an automatically connected CI monitor. Validate with the repository’s own tests, linters and infrastructure tooling.
rows: Run provider validation and same CI check

slides.title: Amazon Q Developer is a companion product
slides.takeaway: Existing guidance, review and transformation workflows are companion services—not DevOps Agent features.
slides.notes: For teams already using Amazon Q Developer, the relevant distinctions are AWS guidance, IDE reviews, GitHub preview workflows and supported transformations. GitHub review triggers differ from other products: subsequent commits do not automatically retrigger a Q review; a new review can be requested explicitly. A language transformation is constrained by its supported source versions, build prerequisites and IDE. These are compatibility decisions, not reasons to represent Q as part of the DevOps Agent runtime.
rows: Preview; use /q review after later commits
Validate build prerequisites and resulting code

slides.title: Pilot a single service with scoped read access
slides.takeaway: Prove the read path before expanding automated effects.
slides.notes: Treat deployment readiness as a team decision. Record the feature’s availability, Agent Space Region, data-source access, mutation paths and stop responsibility. For the first service, leave directed actions off unless a separately reviewed experiment requires them. Put release-preview work in a different pilot lane. The documentation specifies behavior; this checklist is the recommended operating design for the team.

items.title: Boundary
items.body: One service, owned accounts and named operators.

items.title: Evidence
items.body: Known logs, metrics, deployments and repository links.

items.title: Effects
items.body: Read baseline; explicit action approval when enabled.

items.title: Availability
items.body: Production features versus us-east-1 release preview.

items.title: Recovery
items.body: Rollback assumptions and a stop owner.

items.title: Review
items.body: Source checks before escalation or sharing.

slides.title: Pilot metrics require verified engineering results
slides.takeaway: Measure review effort and rework for independently accepted outcomes.
slides.notes: The scorecard is a proposal, not an AWS performance claim. Use the same small set of representative tasks before and during the pilot. Measure how much time an engineer spends reaching an evidence-supported hypothesis, how often conclusions need correction, and whether recommended prevention work is accepted. Count service and integration consumption as well as human review effort. Do not infer production MTTR improvement from a staged demo.
rows: Validate access and a historical incident
Accept one improvement and one report
Repeat tasks; inspect risk and cost

slides.title: Accept outcomes only after verification and authorization
slides.takeaway: Investigate with context. Gate the effect. Close with independent verification.
slides.notes: Close by asking the team to choose one read-heavy operational workflow and its owner. The agent can help connect evidence and produce useful recommendations, but the engineer remains responsible for the decision and its consequences. Release preview, directed actions and active tests should each be evaluated on their own terms. Questions follow the timed close. The detailed inventory below maps every original capability to the new presentation so no feature disappears during the restructuring.

items.title: Start
items.body: One service and a reproducible incident snapshot.

items.title: Keep
items.body: Existing release, approval and incident ownership.

items.title: Require
items.body: Source-backed conclusions and an explicit next action.
